name: Imru' al-Qays
bio: Imru' al-Qays ibn Hujr, of the royal Kinda clan of Akil al-Murar, was born in Najd or Yemen around 497 CE; his father was king over the tribes of Asad and Ghatafan, and his maternal uncle, the poet al-Muhalhil, taught him to compose. He made verses as a boy and lived for pleasure, so his father sent him away, and when Banu Asad killed his father he said: “He left me to waste when I was small and loaded his blood on me when I was grown. No sobriety today and no drunkenness tomorrow: today wine, tomorrow the deed”, and set out for revenge. He made the first of the Mu'allaqat, “Qifa nabki”, and Ibn Sallam reports that those who ranked him first said he was the first to do things later poets copied, such as halting his companions to weep at an abandoned camp, and that he excelled at simile; asked who was the greatest poet, Labid answered: “The wandering king.” Hunted by al-Mundhir, king of Iraq, on Persia's orders, he took refuge with al-Samaw'al and then went to the Byzantine emperor in Constantinople for help against Persia, and was made governor of Palestine. On the way there sores broke out on his body and he died at Ankara around 545 CE, some eighty years before the Hijra, which earned him the name Dhu al-Quruh, “the man of the sores”.
